name: Weight-loss jabs (GLP-1) for face leaning

lead: GLP-1 weight-loss injections such as semaglutide lower appetite and body weight, and some people in looksmaxxing and aesthetic circles use them to get a leaner, more defined face where bone structure shows.

The chain is fat loss: the drugs mimic the gut hormone GLP-1, reducing appetite and slowing gastric emptying, and as body fat falls, facial fat falls with it. In a phase III trial of 1,961 adults with obesity, mean weight change at 68 weeks was about -14.9% with semaglutide versus -2.4% with placebo. Face leaning is a by-product of general weight loss; no drug in this class is approved for reducing facial fat. Recent reviews discuss 'Ozempic face', the hollow or aged look that can follow rapid fat loss.

paras: These are prescription injectables used over months, usually with diet and exercise changes. People who want a leaner face typically watch the pace of loss and pair it with strength training to keep muscle.

Common effects include nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea; gallstones and a boxed thyroid-tumour warning (from rodent studies) are listed. They are prescription-only, and the FDA says compounded forms have not been shown safe or effective.

angle.text: GLP-1 jabs cut appetite, body fat falls, and the face slims so bone structure shows. Trials measured body weight rather than faces, and rapid loss can also bring the hollowing popularly called 'Ozempic face'.

lead: Weight-loss jabs are injectable GLP-1 receptor agonist medicines, such as semaglutide (sold as Ozempic and Wegovy) and the dual GIP/GLP-1 agonist tirzepatide (Mounjaro and Zepbound), that reduce appetite and body weight. People in looksmaxxing and aesthetic-medicine circles use them to get leaner: as body fat falls, the face loses fat too, and proponents say this sharpens the jawline, cheekbones and under-eye area. The flip side of rapid facial fat loss is popularly called "Ozempic face."[1][2][3]

Semaglutide was approved in the US for type 2 diabetes in December 2017 and, at a higher dose, for weight management in June 2021 [1]. In the phase III STEP 1 trial of 1,961 adults with overweight or obesity, mean weight change at 68 weeks was -14.9% with semaglutide versus -2.4% with placebo [4]. In SURMOUNT-1, 2,539 adults given tirzepatide lost a mean of 15.0% to 20.9% of body weight at 72 weeks depending on dose, versus 3.1% with placebo [5]. Face leaning is a by-product of general weight loss rather than a targeted effect; no drug in this class is approved for reducing facial fat.

Published clinical literature on the face specifically is mostly narrative and systematic reviews, case series and surgeon commentaries rather than controlled trials. A 2025 systematic review of 23 plastic-surgery articles describes the changes as resembling advanced aging, and a Google Trends analysis links searches for the term to rising interest in facial fillers and plastic surgeons [6][7]. Several 2026 papers discuss whether "Ozempic face" is a distinct clinical entity and how rapid weight loss affects facial ageing [8].

paras: Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article lists GLP-1 drugs among peptides discussed in the community and among substances used off-label under the heading of hardmaxxing, noting that people without a medical indication may obtain them through a grey market of unregulated products, and lists stomach, pancreas and gallbladder problems among the risks.[2]

The appeal in appearance terms is leanness. Looksmaxxers commonly name hollow cheeks, a defined jawline and visible cheekbones as desirable features [2], and lowering body fat is the usual route to them. Proponents argue that GLP-1 drugs make a calorie deficit easier to sustain because appetite falls, so the face slims along with the body. Aesthetic clinicians and surgeons describe the same fat loss as a possible cause of hollowing, skin laxity and an older look, particularly in people who lose weight rapidly.[8][6]

A looksmax.org thread comparing semaglutide, tirzepatide and retatrutide says appetite control accounts for roughly 90 percent of the challenge of fat loss and presents these drugs as a way to manage it.[9] T Nation hosted a feature asking whether semaglutide is a "miracle" fat-loss drug, noting that celebrities were reported to have used it to get leaner.[10]

Wikipedia traces GLP-1 research to the 1970s and 1980s work of Jens Juul Holst and Joel Habener, with the hormone's significant effects found in 1988. Michael Nauck's 1993 infusion of GLP-1 in people with type 2 diabetes normalised blood glucose but caused significant side effects. Novo Nordisk researchers led by Lotte Bjerre Knudsen developed liraglutide in 1998, and a Novo team later developed semaglutide as a longer-acting alternative, with a phase II trial starting in June 2008.[1]

Ozempic was approved in the US for type 2 diabetes in December 2017, followed by Canada, the EU and Japan in 2018. Oral Rybelsus was approved in the US in September 2019, and Wegovy, the higher-dose injection for weight management, in June 2021 (EU January 2022). In December 2025 the FDA approved an oral version for weight management under the Wegovy name.[1]

Tirzepatide's Mounjaro was approved in the US for type 2 diabetes in May 2022 and Zepbound for chronic weight management in November 2023; the UK regulator extended Mounjaro's indication to weight management the same month.[11]

Semaglutide mimics the gut hormone GLP-1. As described in the looksmax.org comparison thread, the drug slows stomach emptying, reduces hunger through effects on the brain and boosts insulin production; the same thread says tirzepatide also targets GIP and retatrutide adds a third hormone receptor.[9] Retatrutide is an investigational triple agonist of GIP, GLP-1 and glucagon receptors whose phase 2 trial in adults with obesity was published in 2023.[12]

Wikipedia describes the most common adverse effects of semaglutide as nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, constipation and abdominal pain that peak during the first 8 to 12 weeks of dose escalation, and notes that delayed gastric emptying can rarely cause gastroparesis or bowel obstruction.[1]

sections.h: Facial changes with rapid weight loss
paras: The term "Ozempic face" emerged in popular media in the early 2020s as semaglutide prescribing grew. New York dermatologist Paul Jarrod Frank, who is credited with coining it, told Fortune in January 2023 that he sees it "every day in patients," and Dallas dermatologist Elizabeth Houshmand described patients complaining that their faces look gaunt and have lost volume. New York plastic surgeon Oren Tepper said weight loss "tends to turn your facial clock forward." [3]

Reviews generally attribute the appearance to loss of facial fat pads and skin elasticity associated with weight loss in general, as also seen after bariatric surgery and other rapid weight loss, rather than to a drug-specific effect; this remains under discussion.[8][13] A 2024 Journal of Drugs in Dermatology commentary frames the question as whether Ozempic face is a novel adverse effect or a natural consequence of rapid weight loss, and says dermatologists are well placed to counsel patients starting or stopping these drugs.[13] Other 2023 to 2024 papers by facial plastic surgeons describe it as a new challenge for their practice and analyse trends and treatment difficulties.[14][15]

Reported responses include injectable fillers and fat transfer, facelifts, and energy-based devices. A 2025 case series from Italy reported on 24 patients treated with subdermal bipolar radiofrequency after GLP-1-associated facial changes, with most rating their satisfaction positively at follow-up of at least 12 months.[16] Public interest in the topic has been measurable: Google Trends searches for Ozempic face terms rose significantly between June 2022 and June 2025, alongside searches for facial volume procedures.[7] CNN reported in July 2025 that the phenomenon may be driving a cosmetic surgery boom in the US.[17]

Weight lost on GLP-1 drugs includes some lean mass as well as fat. A 2025 network meta-analysis of 22 randomized trials (2,258 participants) found GLP-1 receptor agonists reduced body weight by about 3.6 kg on average, with fat mass falling by about 3 kg and lean mass by under 1 kg; lean mass made up roughly a quarter of total weight lost, while relative lean mass was unchanged.[18] A separate 2025 meta-analysis of nine placebo-controlled trials with DXA scans estimated that about 30 percent of weight lost with these drugs is lean mass.[19] A SURMOUNT-1 DXA substudy of 160 participants found body weight fell 21.3% with tirzepatide, with fat mass down 33.9% and lean mass down 10.9%, and the proportion of weight lost as fat or lean mass was consistent across subgroups.[20]

A 2025 review by Mechanick and colleagues says trial participants lost 10 percent or more of their muscle mass over 68 to 72 weeks and recommends adequate protein and resistance training to limit muscle loss.[21] Looksmaxxing posters who write about these drugs often describe pairing them with training to keep muscle while dieting.[9] Wikipedia notes a 2024 systematic review in which lean mass loss ranged from negligible to substantial across studies while the ratio of lean to total mass rose.[1]

Common effects are nausea, diarrhoea, vomiting, constipation and abdominal pain, typically peaking during dose escalation. Gallstones are a recognised risk, and the US label carries a boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumours based on rodent studies; the drugs are contraindicated with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN2.[1] Wikipedia also reports early worsening of diabetic retinopathy linked to rapid glucose lowering, and that in January 2026 the FDA requested removal of the suicidal-behaviour warning from GLP-1 labels.[1] A Lemmy thread reported that the FDA added a rare vision-loss warning to popular GLP-1 drugs.[22]

For tirzepatide, Wikipedia lists nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, decreased appetite and constipation as common, with rates rising with dose, and reports that the UK regulator warned in 2026 of a small risk of severe acute pancreatitis.[11]

In the STEP 1 off-treatment extension (327 participants), those who had taken semaglutide regained 11.6 percentage points of their lost weight in the year after withdrawal, about two-thirds of their prior loss, and cardiometabolic improvements reverted towards baseline; the authors concluded that ongoing treatment is required to maintain benefits.[23] Wikipedia cites a 2025 review finding people regain on average about 67 percent of lost weight within a year of stopping semaglutide, and reports about 53 percent regain after stopping tirzepatide in one study.[1][11] For appearance, proponents and critics alike note that facial changes track the weight trajectory.

The FDA declared shortages of Ozempic and Wegovy from August 2022, and compounding pharmacies prepared versions under the shortage rules. The FDA states that compounded semaglutide salt forms have not been shown to be safe or effective and that it does not evaluate compounded drugs.[1][24] Tirzepatide was declared in shortage in December 2022 and the FDA declared the shortage over in October 2024.[11]

The FDA's public concerns page says unapproved versions are not reviewed for safety, effectiveness or quality, that compounded drugs should be used only when an approved drug cannot meet a patient's needs, and that counterfeit Ozempic has been found in the US supply. It also says products labelled "for research purposes" or "not for human consumption" containing semaglutide, tirzepatide, retatrutide, survodutide or mazdutide have been sold for human use, and that retatrutide cannot be used in compounding under federal law. As of May 31, 2026 it had received more than 990 adverse event reports for compounded semaglutide and more than 730 for compounded tirzepatide, with the agency noting under-reporting is likely.[24] Counterfeit Ozempic pens, possibly containing insulin, were reported in Europe in October 2023, with several hospitalisations, and the FDA warned about counterfeits in December 2023.[1]

In 2026 Hacker News users discussed an FDA statement of intent to take action against non-approved GLP-1 products.[25] In the US, Wikipedia reports a 2022 Wegovy list price of $1,349 per month and a US semaglutide patent expiry no earlier than December 2031; patents have expired in India and Brazil in 2026 and generics have been approved in Canada.[1]

Coverage of the drugs has been shaped by celebrity reports and by debate over fairness. Fortune's 2023 explainer noted that Novo Nordisk says it does not promote off-label use and that off-label demand has contributed to shortages and to criticism that patients who need the drug for its approved purpose cannot get it.[3] Wikipedia's semaglutide article describes public perception of the drugs as an "easy way out", and Danish research on patients tinkering with doses and fighting for access.[1] T Nation's feature framed semaglutide as a celebrity fat-loss drug in 2022.[10]

Trials of semaglutide and tirzepatide measured body weight and metabolic outcomes, not facial appearance. STEP 1 (published March 2021) reported -14.9% versus -2.4% body weight at week 68 [4]; SURMOUNT-1 (2022) reported -15.0%, -19.5% and -20.9% at three tirzepatide dose levels versus -3.1% with placebo at week 72 [5]. No controlled trial has measured facial fat or attractiveness as an outcome; facial effects appear only in reviews, case series and commentary.[8][6]

Newer agents are also being studied for weight: a phase 3 trial of orforglipron, an oral small-molecule GLP-1 agonist, examined weight outcomes over 72 weeks in adults with obesity.[26] A phase 2 trial of retatrutide, a triple agonist, ran for 48 weeks in adults with obesity.[12]

Face leaning with these drugs sits alongside other leanness practices discussed in the community, including dieting, cardio and resistance training to keep muscle, and buccal fat removal, which targets the cheeks surgically rather than through overall fat loss.[3] Where facial volume is lost, fillers and fat transfer are the procedures reported in the literature.[6]

SURMOUNT-1 reports up to 20.9% weight loss with tirzepatide; Mounjaro approved in May; FDA begins listing Ozempic and Wegovy as in shortage in August, expanding compounding.[1][5][11]
